# Architecture

How the stack is put together: which layer may depend on which, where chip-, MCU- and product-specific code lives, and
what drivers, kb-core, kb-hal-common, board HALs and products each own. The include tables are on Layers; the per-layer
pages under Standards hold the detail. Rules marked guide are design advice for review.

## KB-ARCH-001: Dependencies point down the stack only { #kb-arch-001 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware, template · since 1.0

No layer includes, links or calls anything above it in the stack on Layers (product, board HAL with its bind, kb-core
handlers, interfaces, rtos, utils, drivers). Each file includes only what the Layers include table allows for its
folder.

*Why:* An upward dependency makes a lower layer untestable without the one above and lets lock, lifecycle and error
mapping be bypassed. Downward-only dependencies let any driver sit under any product.

*Verified by:*

- `include-graph/all` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its folder;
  the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- review: Every new include is allowed by the Layers include table for the folder it is in.

*See also:* [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md); IEC 62304:2006+A1:2015 5.3.2 (interfaces between software
items)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#includes)

## KB-ARCH-002: A layer skip is a defect even when it works { #kb-arch-002 }

**MUST** · library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Code that reaches past the layer directly below it (a manager calling a driver through a handler's driver pointer, an
application calling an `Esp*` class or raw FreeRTOS, middleware including a handler) is fixed by adding the missing call
to the skipped layer, not by allowing the skip.

*Why:* The skipped layer's lock, lifecycle and error mapping silently stop applying.

*Verified by:*

- `hal-lint/driver-access` (planned): the kb-hal-common lints run in a board HAL's or product's CI; the parameter names
  the lint (boundary, driver-access, allocation, lock)
- review: No call reaches past the layer below it; a missing feature is added to the skipped layer.

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#layer-skips-are-defects)

## KB-ARCH-003: The submodule graph is acyclic and points down { #kb-arch-003 }

!!! note "Proposed"

    Warns until 2027-03-01, then fails CI.

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0 · enforced from 2027-03-01

Submodules point only down the stack: a product pins its board HAL, a board HAL pins kb-hal-common and kb-core, and
kb-core pins drivers. No repository pins one above it or forms a cycle.

*Verified by:*

- `submodule-graph` (planned): walking .gitmodules across the org's repositories finds no cycle and no submodule that
  points up the stack (product -&gt; board HAL -&gt; kb-hal-common and kb-core -&gt; drivers)

*See also:* [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-submodule-pinning-and-tags.md); [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#the-stack)

## KB-ARCH-004: Inside kb-core: utils, then rtos, then interfaces, then handlers { #kb-arch-004 }

!!! note "Proposed"

    Warns until 2027-03-01, then fails CI.

**MUST** · library · since 1.0 · enforced from 2027-03-01

kb-core's parts are the separate CMake targets `kb::utils`, `kb::rtos`, `kb::interfaces` and `kb::handlers`, and each
links only the targets before it in that order, so an upward include fails to build.

*Verified by:*

- `layer-deps` (planned): kb-core's CMake targets link only downward (kb::utils &lt;- kb::rtos &lt;- kb::interfaces
  &lt;- kb::handlers), read from the CMake file API, and each builds alone with KB\_MCU=NONE and KB\_MCU=HOST

*See also:* [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/library.md](../standards/library.md#every-part-of-kb-core)

## KB-ARCH-005: Drivers and kb-core meet only in the handler adapter { #kb-arch-005 }

**MUST** · driver, library, template · since 1.0

A driver depends on nothing in kb-core or any other Kokeb Labs repository; `kb_core_min` in `driver.yml` is its only
mention of kb-core. kb-core's utils, rtos and interfaces never depend on a driver. The handler's adapter, which
implements the driver's port with `Base*` calls, is the one place they meet.

*Why:* A driver must be usable and forkable without anything else from the org, and the core must not change when a chip
is added.

*Verified by:*

- `host-tests` (implemented): the unit tests build and pass on the host with gcc and clang
- `include-graph/driver` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its
  folder; the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- review: Driver code names nothing from kb-core; kb-core code outside handlers/ includes no driver header.

*See also:* [ADR-0012](../adr/0012-unbranded-drivers.md); [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#the-stack)

## KB-ARCH-006: Port hooks move raw bytes; the driver never configures the bus { #kb-arch-006 }

**MUST** · driver, template · since 1.0

Port hooks transfer bytes and nothing else; register addresses travel in the payload. The driver does not set bus speed,
mode or pins: the port or the board does.

*Verified by:*

- review: No driver code or hook argument configures bus speed, mode or pins.

*See also:* [ADR-0003](../adr/0003-crtp-ports.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/driver.md](../standards/driver.md)

## KB-ARCH-007: Drivers never lock, sleep or call an RTOS { #kb-arch-007 }

**MUST** · driver, template · since 1.0

A driver is not thread-safe: it takes no lock, creates no task and calls no RTOS (waiting is KB-CPP-041). The kb-core
handler that owns it does the locking.

*Why:* One owner for locking avoids double locks and lets the same driver run bare-metal or on any RTOS.

*Verified by:*

- `host-tests` (implemented): the unit tests build and pass on the host with gcc and clang
- `include-graph/driver` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its
  folder; the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- review: The driver has no lock, task or RTOS call.

*See also:* [ADR-0003](../adr/0003-crtp-ports.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/driver.md](../standards/driver.md#memory-and-threads)

## KB-ARCH-008: Only a chip's driver and handler know its registers { #kb-arch-008 }

**MUST** · library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

A chip's register map, start-up sequence and quirks live in its driver and its handler only. Managers, HALs and products
use the handler's typed API or `VisitDriver()` and never name a register.

*Verified by:*

- review: No code outside the chip's driver and handler names its registers or bit fields.

*See also:* [ADR-0014](../adr/0014-three-kinds-of-specific.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#three-kinds-of-specific)

## KB-ARCH-009: MCU-specific code lives only in the selected family's folders { #kb-arch-009 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Code that knows an MCU family lives only in kb-core's `interfaces/mcu/<family>/`, a board HAL's `bsp_bind/<family>/` and
a product's `platform/`. The build compiles only the selected family's folders, and every other folder compiles for
every family and on the host.

*Why:* KB-CPP-016 bans the platform macros that would let MCU code hide elsewhere; this rule says where it goes.

*Verified by:*

- `include-graph/mcu` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its folder;
  the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- review: New MCU-specific code is in an `mcu/<family>/`, `bsp_bind/<family>/` or `platform/` folder.

*See also:* [ADR-0014](../adr/0014-three-kinds-of-specific.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#mcu-specific-code)

## KB-ARCH-010: Product-specific needs reach kb-core and drivers only as generic extension points { #kb-arch-010 }

**MUST** · driver, library, template · since 1.0

Nothing in kb-core or a driver is specific to one product: no product macro, pin, channel choice, limit, profile table
or fault catalogue. A product need becomes a config mask, a table passed in as `std::span`, a `Base*` backend interface
or an injected logger, or it stays in the product's board HAL.

*Why:* Whatever one product puts in the core, every other product carries. The second-product test catches it before
merge.

*Verified by:*

- review: A second, made-up product with a different board could use this change to kb-core or the driver without
  editing it.

*See also:* [ADR-0014](../adr/0014-three-kinds-of-specific.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md#product-specific-code)

## KB-ARCH-011: Virtual functions only at the three run-time boundaries { #kb-arch-011 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, template · since 1.0

Virtual functions appear only in kb-core's `Base*` peripheral interfaces, kb-hal-common's `ManagerBase`, `FacadeBase`
and their sink interfaces, and kb-core's `BaseThread` and `BaseThreadsManager`. Drivers, ports, handlers and utilities
have none; code above the bind holds a `Base*&`.

*Why:* Static dispatch keeps drivers and handlers inlined and checkable at compile time; the two run-time boundaries are
where the concrete type is not known until the board is built (the MCU object, the board's managers).

*Verified by:*

- `forbidden-patterns/virtual-outside-interfaces` (implemented): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the
  parameter names the pattern set
- review: A new virtual function is in one of the three boundaries of ADR-0016, nowhere else.

*See also:* [ADR-0016](../adr/0016-virtual-functions.md); [ADR-0003](../adr/0003-crtp-ports.md);
[ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/library.md](../standards/library.md#interfaces)

## KB-ARCH-012: A peripheral only one MCU family has gets a Base\* interface and a gate row { #kb-arch-012 }

**MUST** · driver, library · since 1.0

A peripheral that only one family has (the ESP32 RMT) gets a `Base*` interface in `interfaces/base/` and an
implementation in that family's folder only. A driver that needs it stays platform-free, names the family and peripheral
in `driver.yml`, says it is MCU-bound in its README and Contract page, and becomes a row in the MCU gate table.

*Verified by:*

- review: The peripheral has a `Base*` interface, one family implementation, a `driver.yml` entry and an MCU gate row;
  the driver's `inc/` and `src/` include no vendor SDK.

*See also:* [ADR-0014](../adr/0014-three-kinds-of-specific.md); [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-submodule-pinning-and-tags.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/driver.md](../standards/driver.md#mcu-bound-drivers)

## KB-ARCH-013: A protocol client follows the driver contract except the chip rules { #kb-arch-013 }

**SHOULD** · driver · since 1.0

A driver for a device reached over a protocol (a CANopen node) skips the chip-ID check, register model, datasheet
defaults and register mock, and follows the rest of the driver contract. Its `Initialize()` checks the remote identity
(device type, vendor ID).

*Verified by:*

- review: The client checks the remote identity in Initialize() and otherwise follows the driver contract.

*Explained in:* [standards/driver.md](../standards/driver.md#protocol-clients)

## KB-ARCH-014: Split a large chip into sub-object facades that share the driver { #kb-arch-014 }

**GUIDE** · driver · since 1.0

A chip with many subsystems may expose them as sub-object facades held by the driver
(`driver.telemetry().ReadSupplyMv()`). Each facade follows the driver contract and shares the driver's port, lifecycle
and `Error`.

*Explained in:* [standards/driver.md](../standards/driver.md#large-chips)

## KB-ARCH-015: utils take locks and clocks as arguments; CANopen frames are values { #kb-arch-015 }

**MUST** · library · since 1.0

A kb-core `utils` helper that needs a lock or a clock takes it as a parameter or template argument instead of reaching
up to `kb/rtos/` or the interfaces. `utils/canopen` depends on no CAN interface or driver, does not allocate, and builds
frames as values the caller sends.

*Verified by:*

- `include-graph/utils` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its folder;
  the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- review: A new utils helper takes its lock or clock as an argument; CANopen helpers return frames by value.

*Explained in:* [standards/library.md](../standards/library.md#utils)

## KB-ARCH-016: The kb-core logger is the one logging API above the bind { #kb-arch-016 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Code above the bind logs only through the kb-core logger, whose sink the board HAL injects at start-up. kb-core prints
nothing on its own and carries no product's log format; drivers do not format log text.

*Verified by:*

- `forbidden-patterns/direct-logging` (planned): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the parameter names
  the pattern set
- review: No `printf`, `ESP_LOG*` or vendor logging call above the bind; logging goes through the kb-core logger.

*Explained in:* [standards/library.md](../standards/library.md#handlers)

## KB-ARCH-017: Raw pin numbers appear only in the board's pin table and its bind { #kb-arch-017 }

**MUST** · library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

The `pincfg` framework holds no board's pins. MCU pin numbers appear only in a board HAL's pin table under
`board/<board>/` and in its bind; managers and everything above use functional pin names.

*Verified by:*

- `forbidden-patterns/raw-pins` (planned): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the parameter names the
  pattern set
- review: No `GPIO_NUM_*` or literal pin number outside the board pin table and `bsp_bind/`.

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#board-config)

## KB-ARCH-018: Adapters are mechanical and build on the shared adapter bases { #kb-arch-018 }

**SHOULD** · library · since 1.0

A handler's adapter derives from the shared base in `handlers/common/` for its bus (`HalSpiCommBase`, `HalI2cCommBase`,
`HalUartCommBase`), which holds the bus reference, pin mapping and delay and log hooks, and adds only what is
chip-specific. Retry policy and other decisions live in the handler, not the adapter.

*Verified by:*

- review: The adapter uses the shared base for its bus and contains translation only.

*Explained in:* [standards/handler.md](../standards/handler.md#the-adapter)

## KB-ARCH-019: A driver feature reached through VisitDriver in two places becomes a typed method { #kb-arch-019 }

**SHOULD** · library · since 1.0

When the same driver feature is used through `VisitDriver()` in more than one place, the handler gains a typed method
for it.

*Verified by:*

- review: No driver feature is reached through VisitDriver() in two places without a typed handler method.

*Explained in:* [standards/handler.md](../standards/handler.md#driver-access)

## KB-ARCH-020: A board HAL never copies kb-hal-common; shared managers move there { #kb-arch-020 }

**MUST** · hal · since 1.0

kb-hal-common holds the manager and facade bases, the bind interface, the common managers and the lints; a board HAL
holds only its board config, pin table, bind and board-specific managers. A board HAL carries no copy of kb-hal-common
code, and a manager two boards need moves to kb-hal-common.

*Why:* Copied managers drift; the review behind ADR-0005 found six near-copies.

*Verified by:*

- `duplicate-code` (planned): jscpd finds no block in a board HAL that duplicates kb-hal-common code above the
  configured threshold
- review: The HAL adds no copy of a kb-hal-common class; a manager a second board needs is moved there.

*See also:* [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#what-lives-where)

## KB-ARCH-021: Common managers take board specifics as configuration and never name a board { #kb-arch-021 }

**MUST** · hal, library · since 1.0

The managers in kb-hal-common receive everything board-specific (channels, LEDs, NVS namespaces) as configuration and
contain no board or product name.

*Verified by:*

- `forbidden-patterns/board-names` (planned): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the parameter names the
  pattern set
- review: No board or product name or board-specific constant in kb-hal-common.

*See also:* [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#managers)

## KB-ARCH-022: One manager per board function, owning its handlers { #kb-arch-022 }

**MUST** · hal · since 1.0

A board HAL has one manager per board function; the manager owns that function's handlers and the `Base*` objects the
bind created for them. A new chip in an existing category, a board variant or a cross-category feature extends an
existing manager rather than adding one.

*Verified by:*

- review: A new manager covers a board function no existing manager covers.

*See also:* [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#managers)

## KB-ARCH-023: The facade starts managers in a fixed, documented order { #kb-arch-023 }

**MUST** · hal · since 1.0

The board facade derives from `FacadeBase` and passes its managers in a start-up order fixed at compile time. The order,
and why, is on the HAL's Architecture page; managers do not start each other.

*Verified by:*

- review: The start order is a compile-time list passed to FacadeBase and matches the Architecture page.

*See also:* [ADR-0002](../adr/0002-lifecycle.md); [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#facade-and-start-up)

## KB-ARCH-024: Start-up fails closed and leaves every actuator safe { #kb-arch-024 }

**MUST** · hal, firmware · since 1.0

`Initialize()` stops at the first failing manager, deinitialises the ones already started in reverse order and returns
the failing manager and its status. Only managers the board can run without are optional, never safety-relevant ones;
after a failed start-up the product reports the fault and starts no control task.

*Why:* A half-started board with a live actuator and no supervising task is the dangerous case.

*Verified by:*

- `hal-startup-test` (planned): a HAL host test with the host bind injects a failure into each manager in turn and
  checks that start-up stops, deinitialises the started managers in reverse and reports the failing ManagerId
- review: A host test injects a failure into each manager in turn and checks the reverse deinitialisation; no
  safety-relevant manager is optional.

*See also:* [ADR-0002](../adr/0002-lifecycle.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#facade-and-start-up)

## KB-ARCH-025: The facade is the product's only way into the board { #kb-arch-025 }

**MUST** · hal, firmware · since 1.0

The application uses only the HAL facade and its managers' public API, `kb::rtos` and the kb-core logger. The facade
exposes managers by reference and nothing below them.

*Verified by:*

- `hal-lint/boundary` (planned): the kb-hal-common lints run in a board HAL's or product's CI; the parameter names the
  lint (boundary, driver-access, allocation, lock)
- review: The application reaches hardware only through the facade and its managers.

*See also:* [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/product.md](../standards/product.md#what-the-application-uses)

## KB-ARCH-026: The bind is the only HAL code that names the MCU family { #kb-arch-026 }

**MUST** · hal · since 1.0

In a board HAL only `bsp_bind/<family>/` names MCU types. It implements the one bind interface declared in kb-hal-common
by creating kb-core's `interfaces/mcu/<family>/` objects; it never reimplements a peripheral, and a peripheral kb-core
lacks is added to kb-core first.

*Verified by:*

- `hal-lint/boundary` (planned): the kb-hal-common lints run in a board HAL's or product's CI; the parameter names the
  lint (boundary, driver-access, allocation, lock)
- review: The bind creates kb-core MCU objects and contains no peripheral implementation of its own.

*See also:* [ADR-0005](../adr/0005-kb-hal-common.md); [ADR-0014](../adr/0014-three-kinds-of-specific.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#the-platform-bind)

## KB-ARCH-027: A board function the facade lacks is added to the HAL first { #kb-arch-027 }

**SHOULD** · firmware, hal · since 1.0

When the application needs a board function the facade does not offer (for example CAN), it is added to the board HAL
and then used; the application does not reach around the facade for it.

*Verified by:*

- review: New board access in the application goes through a facade or manager method.

*Explained in:* [standards/product.md](../standards/product.md#what-the-application-uses)

## KB-ARCH-028: Application logic lives in the application, not in platform/ or the HAL { #kb-arch-028 }

**MUST** · firmware, hal · since 1.0

A product's `platform/` holds `app_main()`, partitions, OTA and the console. `app_main()` creates the facade,
initialises it, reports a failed start-up and starts the tasks. Behaviour (tasks, protocols, state machines, faults)
lives in the application, never in `platform/` or the board HAL.

*Verified by:*

- review: platform/ and the HAL contain start-up and board code only, no application behaviour.

*Explained in:* [standards/product.md](../standards/product.md#platform)

## KB-ARCH-029: Run-time faults follow the fault catalogue's reaction { #kb-arch-029 }

**GUIDE** · hal, firmware · since 1.0

Detect bus and device faults, and react as the product's fault catalogue says (stop, derate, warn) rather than ad hoc.
Degraded operation is a designed reaction listed in the catalogue; start-up stays fail-closed.

*Explained in:* [standards/product.md](../standards/product.md#faults)

## KB-ARCH-030: A safety-classified product records its classification and what it implies { #kb-arch-030 }

**SHOULD** · firmware (safety level and above) · since 1.0

A product meant for a safety-classified use records its software safety class (IEC 62304 class, SIL or ASIL), the
reasoning, and the verification that class requires, in its own ADRs.

*Verified by:*

- review: The product's docs/adr/ has a classification record naming the class and the verification it needs.

*See also:* IEC 62304:2006+A1:2015 4.3 (software safety classification)

*Explained in:* [assurance-levels.md](../assurance-levels.md)

## KB-ARCH-031: Only kb-core rtos includes RTOS headers; everything above uses kb::rtos { #kb-arch-031 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Drivers, utils and pincfg use no RTOS. Only kb-core's `rtos/` backend folders include RTOS headers; handlers, HALs and
products use `kb::rtos` only, and only the bind and a product's `platform/` may call the SDK or RTOS directly.

*Verified by:*

- `include-graph/rtos` (planned): every #include in library code is allowed by the Layers include table for its folder;
  the parameter names the layer (driver, utils, rtos, interfaces, mcu, handlers, hal, product) or `all`
- `forbidden-patterns/raw-rtos` (planned): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the parameter names the
  pattern set
- review: No raw RTOS call or header, `std::mutex` or `std::thread` above the bind.

*See also:* [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/threading-and-timing.md](../standards/threading-and-timing.md#who-may-call-the-rtos)

## KB-ARCH-032: Only the product or a HAL manager creates tasks { #kb-arch-032 }

**MUST** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Tasks are created through `kb::rtos` (`BaseThread`, `BaseThreadsManager`) by the product or a HAL manager, never by a
handler or a driver.

*Verified by:*

- `forbidden-patterns/task-creation` (planned): a source scan for a construct the handbook bans; the parameter names the
  pattern set
- review: No handler or driver creates a task.

*Explained in:* [standards/threading-and-timing.md](../standards/threading-and-timing.md#tasks)

## KB-ARCH-033: Core affinity is the product's decision { #kb-arch-033 }

**SHOULD** · hal, firmware · since 1.0

Which core a task runs on is set in the product's task configuration header. HAL code does not assume a dual-core MCU or
pin work to a core.

*Verified by:*

- review: No core affinity is set or assumed outside the product's task configuration.

*Explained in:* [standards/threading-and-timing.md](../standards/threading-and-timing.md#tasks)

## KB-ARCH-034: Handler callbacks run in the caller's task { #kb-arch-034 }

**SHOULD** · library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

A callback from a handler into the product runs in the task that made the call. A callback that must reach another task
posts to an `OsQueue` instead of doing that task's work.

*Verified by:*

- review: Callbacks that cross tasks post to a queue.

*Explained in:* [standards/threading-and-timing.md](../standards/threading-and-timing.md#what-crosses-tasks)

## KB-ARCH-035: kb-core pins each driver to a release tag, with its handler and catalogue entry { #kb-arch-035 }

!!! note "Proposed"

    Warns until 2027-03-01, then fails CI.

**MUST** · library · since 1.0 · enforced from 2027-03-01

kb-core includes each driver as the submodule `drivers/driver-<chip>/` at the commit of a release tag, never through a
package registry. The driver is released and pinned before its handler lands, and every pinned driver has a handler and
an entry in `catalog/compat.yml`.

*Verified by:*

- `kb-core-catalog` (planned): every drivers/driver-&lt;chip&gt; gitlink is the commit of a v\* release tag, has a
  handlers/&lt;chip&gt;/ folder and a catalog/compat.yml entry, and regenerating compat.yml and the MCU gate table from
  the pinned driver.yml files changes nothing

*See also:* [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-submodule-pinning-and-tags.md); [ADR-0013](../adr/0013-kb-core-monorepo.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/release.md](../standards/release.md)

## KB-ARCH-036: The compatibility catalogue is generated from the pinned drivers { #kb-arch-036 }

!!! note "Proposed"

    Warns until 2027-03-01, then fails CI.

**MUST** · library · since 1.0 · enforced from 2027-03-01

`catalog/compat.yml` is built from the `driver.yml` of every pinned driver and generates the MCU gate table in
`cmake/kb_build_settings.cmake`. CI regenerates both and fails on any difference, and kb-core's release notes list the
same driver versions.

*Verified by:*

- `kb-core-catalog` (planned): every drivers/driver-&lt;chip&gt; gitlink is the commit of a v\* release tag, has a
  handlers/&lt;chip&gt;/ folder and a catalog/compat.yml entry, and regenerating compat.yml and the MCU gate table from
  the pinned driver.yml files changes nothing

*See also:* [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-submodule-pinning-and-tags.md)

*Explained in:* [standards/release.md](../standards/release.md)

## KB-ARCH-037: Extend what exists before adding a new entity { #kb-arch-037 }

**GUIDE** · library, hal · since 1.0

Before adding a handler, manager or interface, check whether an existing one should grow. A new chip gets a handler; a
new board function gets a manager; a new chip in an existing function does not.

*Explained in:* [standards/hal.md](../standards/hal.md#managers)

## KB-ARCH-038: Design for bounded memory and cheap bus traffic { #kb-arch-038 }

**GUIDE** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

Batch bus transactions, use DMA for large transfers, pick cache-friendly algorithms, and size pools and buffers at
compile time. Caching is fine; lazy allocation and run-time pools from the heap are not.

*See also:* [ADR-0004](../adr/0004-no-heap.md)


## KB-ARCH-039: Real-time paths have bounded latency and named priorities { #kb-arch-039 }

**GUIDE** · hal, firmware · since 1.0

Code on a real-time path has a known worst-case time, takes no unbounded wait, and runs at a priority named in the
product's task configuration. Resources it needs are reserved at start-up.

*Explained in:* [standards/threading-and-timing.md](../standards/threading-and-timing.md#tasks)

## KB-ARCH-040: Review architecture before details { #kb-arch-040 }

**GUIDE** · driver, library, hal, firmware · since 1.0

A reviewer checks layering, ownership, locking, error mapping, fault reaction and timing before line-level comments, and
a design problem is raised first.

*Explained in:* [standards/layers.md](../standards/layers.md)
